promises.title: Promise: Review the Companies and Allied Matters Act (CAMA) and other legislations to remove barriers that hinder CSOs from delivering on their mandate.
promises.promise_blog:
By prioritizing a review of the Companies and Allied Matters Act (CAMA) and related laws, the HoR recognizes that outdated or overly restrictive legal frameworks can hamper advocacy, service delivery, and civic engagement—calling this a strategic priority by including it in the legislative agenda reflects its importance in reinforcing democratic participation and accountability.

 

The current legal landscape under CAMA poses several barriers to CSOs. For example, the law grants the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC) the sweeping power to remove trustees or appoint interim managers in the public interest—without clear due process. This provision gives the government significant discretionary control over CSOs’ governance and continuity. Additionally, cumbersome registration hurdles—such as mandatory government approval of charitable objectives and lengthy publication requirements—delay or sometimes deter incorporation. Removing these barriers would allow CSOs to more swiftly register, operate, and pursue their mandates—particularly in areas like human rights, governance reform, and public service delivery. 

 

This reform is a significant opportunity to strengthen both civic space and checks and balances in Nigeria. For CSOs, a clearer and more rights-focused legal framework would reduce administrative hurdles and the risk of arbitrary interference. This would also make it easier for them to secure local funding and form partnerships.

 

Ultimately, this reform enhances democratic accountability for everyone. By empowering CSOs to effectively monitor government performance, amplify citizens' voices, and drive progress, the House of Representatives demonstrates its commitment to fostering inclusive and resilient civic participation. This makes it one of the most impactful and enabling promises on the current legislative agenda.
promises.description: Review the Companies and Allied Matters Act (CAMA) and other legislations to remove barriers that hinder CSOs from delivering on their mandate.

promises.title: Mandate the publication of sessional/annual reports detailing House activities, budgets, and outcomes.
promises.promise_blog:
In Nigeria, legislative opacity has long been a challenge. While our National Assembly is one of the best-funded parliaments in Africa, commanding a significant budgetary allocation every year (over ₦344 billion in 2024 according to BudgIT), the budgetary process of the National Assembly itself is notoriously opaque. For many years, the National Assembly’s budget was presented as a single line item in the federal budget, making it impossible for the public to know how the funds were allocated or spent. Only after pressure from civil society and the media did some partial details begin to emerge in recent appropriation cycles. Even then, line-by-line details remain limited, and implementation reports are rare.

 

This opacity makes it almost impossible for citizens to track how billions allocated to the legislature are spent on salaries, constituency projects, website/media, or research. Mandating the publication of sessional or annual reports would bring clarity: Nigerians would see what bills were considered, how committees performed, what oversight activities were carried out, and how legislative resources were spent. Such reporting is standard practice in many democracies and is crucial to bridging the trust gap between legislators and citizens.

 

Sessional and annual reports are not just about financials; they also provide a performance scorecard. Citizens would be able to track whether the House is meeting its legislative objectives, which committees were most active, and what oversight inquiries were conducted. This opens the door for citizen-driven accountability, where civil society, media, and voters can ask the right questions and demand better representation. It would also encourage lawmakers themselves to treat oversight and committee work more seriously, knowing their performance will be documented and judged in public reports.
promises.description: Mandate the publication of sessional/annual reports detailing House activities, budgets, and outcomes.

promises.title: Legislate to increase women’s representation in elective positions by creating special women-only seats in the Senate and House of Representatives and encouraging State Houses of Assembly to do the same
promises.promise_blog:
Nigeria has one of the lowest rates of women’s legislative representation in the world. In the current (10th) National Assembly, women occupy only 4.2 per cent of seats, just 4 Senators and 17 Representatives out of 469 total seats. Even more strikingly, across the entire federation (including state legislatures), women occupy just 64 of 1,460 elective legislative seats according to a recent report. 

These figures reflect deeply entrenched barriers—cultural, financial, institutional—that limit women’s ability to contest competitive open seats. This promise to “legislate to increase women’s representation by creating special women-only seats in the Senate and House and encouraging State Houses of Assembly to do the same” is thus not merely symbolic. It is a structural reform intended to overcome the inertia of status quo bias, reduce the burden of electoral contests in male-dominated primaries, and guarantee a baseline of female inclusion. Also, on the National Assembly Library Trust Fund website, the Deputy Speaker, Hon Benjamin Kalu, has publicly called for support of the reserved seats bill, noting the stark numerical gap (only 15 Women in the Reps, 4 in the Senate). 

Also noteworthy: under HB 1189 sponsored by Hon Kalu, the reserved seats proposal is already before the National Assembly. The bill seeks constitutional alteration to insert special seats for women, adjusting Sections 48, 49, 71, 77, 91, 117, etc. 

HB 1189 envisions adding additional slots for women in both the National and State Assemblies. The bill has been scaled down to 74 seats (i.e 37 seats in each chamber), from the 111 seats proposed by the initial bill introduced in the 9th Assembly, to avoid bloating the legislature.

If passed, HB 1189 could begin to shift the baseline: women would still contest open seats, but these reserved seats would guarantee that even if they fail in direct contests, a minimum presence is ensured. Civil society and advocates see this as a vital corrective given decades of systemic exclusion.
promises.description: Legislate to increase women’s representation in elective positions by creating special women-only seats in the Senate and House of Representatives and encouraging State Houses of Assembly to do the same

promises.title: Promise: Enact Laws that Enhance the Capital Markets's Transparency Liquidity, and Depth to Attract Domestic and Foreign Investors
promises.promise_blog:
The 10th House of Representatives’ pledge to enact laws that enhance the capital market’s transparency, liquidity, and depth addresses critical gaps highlighted in both the NGX-commissioned “Final Report – Nigeria Capital Markets” and broader market observations. The NGX report underscores persistent weaknesses in legal frameworks and enforcement mechanisms that impair transparency and suppress investor confidence.

 

By mandating real-time corporate disclosures, enforcing timely dividend payments, and strengthening compliance with International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS), lawmakers can significantly improve credibility and fairness in the market, a key determinants of domestic and foreign investment. Legislative reforms that facilitate the introduction of exchange-traded funds (ETFs), derivatives, real estate investment trusts (REITs), and securities lending will broaden market offerings. Also, when coupled with digital modernisation—such as electronic IPOs, e-voting, and faster settlement systems—these reforms will deepen market liquidity and resilience, making Nigeria’s capital markets more dynamic, efficient, and attractive to a variety of investors.

 

Moreover, the legislature's actions are already resonating in practice. In a March 2024 hearing, the House Committee on Capital Markets and Institutions questioned market operators about why dividend payments were not made promptly, highlighting the urgency of improving investor protection and trust.

 

By combining these oversight initiatives with robust legal reforms and sustained scrutiny of regulators like the SEC, NGX, and FMDQ, the House of Representatives can drive meaningful transformation. This integrated approach promises to elevate Nigeria’s capital market toward global standards and enhance its competitiveness as a premier investment destination.

promises.title: Promise: Domesticate the relevant international human rights treaties
promises.promise_blog:
In a bid to meet global human rights standards, the 10th HOR made this pledge, underscoring the green chamber’s intent to translate Nigeria’s international obligations into enforceable domestic law. Nigeria operates under a dualist legal system, which means that international treaties, including human rights treaties, don't automatically become part of the country's domestic law just by being signed and ratified.

 

For an international treaty to be enforceable in a Nigerian court, it must first be domesticated, i.e it should be codified into local statutes. This process involves the National Assembly enacting the treaty into a national law. Section 12(1) of the 1999 constitution (amended) stipulates that “no treaty … shall have the force of law except to which any such treaty has been enacted into law by the National Assembly”. This contrasts with a monist system, where international law is automatically part of the domestic legal system upon ratification.

 

Scholars and other legal practitioners have highlighted that this requirement has led to significant gaps between Nigeria’s ratification of treaties and their actual enforcement, creating situations where human rights obligations remain aspirational rather than operational.

Despite the systemic hurdles, Nigeria has successfully domesticated several international instruments, examples being:

  • The Child Rights Act of 2003 &

  • The African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights, which was signed and ratified in 1983

 

This commitment by the House of Representatives to domesticate relevant human rights treaties is a step towards bridging the gap between Nigeria’s international resolutions and tangible domestic protections. By institutionalising treaty domestication, Nigeria can reinforce its adherence to global norms and ensure broader protections for its populace. Leveraging successful models like the Child Rights Act, this pledge could catalyse a more consistent enactment of human rights statutes across states. If combined with oversight mechanisms—such as strengthening the Human Rights Committee and the National Human Rights Commission—the pledge could significantly enhance human rights enforcement in Nigeria’s legal and institutional landscape.
promises.description: Through this bill the HoR aim to align the countrywith to numerous international treaties

promises.title: Promise: Amendment of the Constitution to Review Appointing Powers of Members of the CJN for FJSC and NJC
promises.promise_blog:
The Chief Justice of Nigeria (CJN) wields significant influence over judicial appointments by serving as Chairman of both the National Judicial Council (NJC) and the Federal Judicial Service Commission (FJSC). The NJC, under the 1999 Constitution, is responsible for recommending appointments, promotions, and discipline of judicial officers, while the FJSC advises the NJC on nominations for apex judicial offices such as the CJN, Supreme Court justices, and the President of the Court of Appeal. Because the CJN chairs both bodies, they occupy a central role in shaping the judiciary’s composition and career progression.

 

This concentration of power raises concerns over impartiality and accountability. In practice, the overlap has created opportunities for nepotism, patronage, and favouritism, with documented instances of relatives and close associates of judicial leaders securing appointments. Such influence undermines merit-based selection, erodes public trust, and limits internal checks within the judiciary. The structure effectively allows one individual to dominate two of the most critical appointment bodies, making it difficult to guard against bias without external oversight.

 

This promise by the Tajudeen Abass-led House of Representatives to amend the constitution to address this overlap is laudable, as it checks the excesses of the powers of the CJN.  While Senate confirmation remains the constitutional requirement for appointments to the highest judicial offices, the HoR can initiate reforms like this pledge to limit the overlap of powers, expand external representation in appointment bodies, and demand transparency in selection processes, thereby ensuring greater accountability and safeguarding the judiciary’s independence.
promises.description: Amendment of the constitution to review appointing powers of members of the CJN for FJSC and NJC

promises.promise_blog:
The speedy passage of the Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Act (Amendment) Bill in the tenth Assembly became a matter of huge importance after the controversy that trailed the amendment of the bill in the previous assembly. Therefore, in the Legislative Agenda, Hon. Tajudeen Abbas-led House of Representatives (HoR) pledge to address important sections of the bill and ensure its passage.

 

In the ninth Assembly, the Senate passed the amendment bill but was overwhelmingly rejected by the lower chamber of the house after much consideration. In the amended forwarded by the ninth Senate to the HoR, the bill stripped the Chairman of ICPC of his powers as listed in Sections 4 and 7 of the Principal Act. Furthermore, the amended bill 2023 passed by the Senate re-names Board members as ‘Commissioners’, a moved termed as 'deceitful' especially as it aim to bring appointed board members into the day-to-day running of such an independent agency.

 

A political commentator, Kunle Aderinokun, argued for the importance of passing this amendment act but also called on the legislators to eschew political interference in the setting the laws for an institution setup to address corruption in the country. "it (the amended bill from the ninth Assembly) was designed to ultimately weaken the ICPC from being an effective law enforcement agency in the critical task of investigation and prosecution of crime, recovery of stolen or diverted public assets, and assessment of corruption risk in Ministries, Departments and Agencies," he wrote.

promises.title: Promise: Review the Process of Appointments into INEC Specifically to Minimise the Involvement of the President in Appointment of Chairman and National Commissioners of INEC
promises.promise_blog:
Under Section 154(1) of Nigeria’s 1999 Constitution as amended, the President is empowered to nominate the chairman and national commissioners of the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), subject to Senate confirmation. While this constitutional mechanism has endured, civil society and the general public have increasingly argued that it jeopardises the Commission’s independence by placing too much influence in the hands of the executive.

 

Controversial precedents have reinforced the demand for reform. In 2022, President Buhari’s nomination of Professor Rhoda Gumus as an INEC Commissioner raised concerns, as opposition parties alleged she was a member of the ruling party (APC). More recently, civil rights group SERAP publicly urged President Tinubu to rescind the appointments of at least three alleged APC members as Resident Electoral Commissioners, arguing that partisan nominations erode public confidence and threaten electoral fairness.

 

Responding to these growing concerns, the House of Representatives pledged to review and amend the appointment process, aiming to minimise the President’s involvement in selecting the INEC chairman and national commissioners. This reform could strengthen electoral integrity by introducing greater transparency and credibility, possibly through an independent selection panel or multi-stakeholder vetting process.
promises.description: Review the process of appointments into INEC specifically to divest/minimise the involvement of the President in appointment of Chairman and National Commissioners of INEC

promises.title: Develop a Code of Ethical Conduct for Staff of the House.
promises.promise_blog:
A professional, accountable legislature depends on the integrity and conduct of its staff; without clear standards, sensitive functions such as policy research, procurement, records management, security and communications become vulnerable to abuse, negligence and corruption. A robust Code of Ethical Conduct for House staff is essential to close these gaps: providing unambiguous rules that prevent conflicts of interest, stop misuse of official resources, and guard against partisan or self-serving behaviour while on duty. Clear standards reduce discretion that breeds favoritism, ensure fair procurement, and make it harder for predatory actors to exploit informal channels for personal gain.

 

Beyond prevention, a binding code establishes predictable procedures for reporting and investigating misconduct, ensuring complaints are handled promptly. This is critical to deter bribery, patronage, and collusion with outside contractors—risks that directly erode citizens’ trust. Equally important are defined sanctions and due‑process safeguards: proportionate penalties, rights of appeal and transparent adjudication protect both the institution and staff from arbitrary action while signalling that violations carry real consequences.



Adopting a strict, enforceable Code is not a symbolic act but a strategic necessity: it professionalises the workforce, protects sensitive processes, prevents reputational damage, and restores public confidence. In short, a well‑designed Code of Ethical Conduct transforms standards into enforceable obligations, shielding the legislature from malpractice and ensuring staff behaviour aligns consistently with democratic values and the public interest.

promises.title: Promise: Amendment of the Constitution to Include the Power of Senate to Conduct Public Hearings and Possibility of Refusal to Confirm based on Findings from Objective Public Compaints.
promises.promise_blog:
Under the leadership of Speaker Tajudeen Abbas, the 10th House of Representatives has identified constitutional reform as a top priority, emphasising the need to make the governance process more open and people-centred. On the front burner is the proposal to amend the Constitution to empower the Senate to conduct public hearings on certain key appointments and to allow the possibility of refusing confirmation if findings arise from credible, objective public complaints, thereby effectively expanding legislative oversight into appointment processes.

 

Embedding such a provision into the Constitution would materially enhance transparency, accountability, and public trust in governmental appointments, especially as the trust deficit seems to be widening between citizens and the government. Public hearings give citizens a voice, spotlighting appointees’ fitness, integrity, and qualifications under public scrutiny. This mechanism helps deter unqualified, opaque, or politically motivated appointments, reinforcing the Senate’s role as a democratic check on the executive. It also aligns Nigeria's governance with international best practices that prioritise openness and public participation as safeguards against cronyism and abuse of power.

 

By championing the inclusion of Senate-led public hearings and rejection powers based on public complaints, the HoR is positioning itself to strengthen oversight, elevate public participation in governance, and fortify confidence in Nigeria’s appointment systems. If pursued effectively—through clear timelines, public consultations, and transparent debate—this reform could mark a meaningful expansion of institutional checks and deepen democratic governance across the federation.

promises.title: Promise: Enact stringent regulations to protect passengers' rights concerning flight delays, cancellations, lost baggage, and other grievances.
promises.promise_blog:
Nigerians have regularly complained about the disregard for passengers' rights by both local and international airlines. In most cases, local travellers are always seen on social media platforms sharing the undignified experiences which they are forced to go through at airports due to disregard for consumer rights by airline operators in Nigeria. This particular issue, of course, has gained the attention of lawmakers whenever there is a huge public outcry, but in many instances, they are not adequately addressed.

 

Thus, one of the important pledges of the 10th Assembly of the House of Representatives is to 'enact stringent regulations to protect passengers' rights concerning flight delays, cancellations, lost baggage, and other grievances'. According to the Nigeria Civil Aviation Authority (NCAA) the issue of flight disruptions in Nigeria reached a new high between September and October 2024 with about 5,225 delays and 190 cancellations out of 10,804 flights that operated in both months.

 

Since their inauguration of the 10th Assembly, legislators have shown efforts toward combating the systemic problems within the aviation sector. In October 2023, the lawmakers condemned the ill-treatment of passengers by airlines by asking the aviation authorities to develop policies and regulations to protect and preserve the rights of air travellers in Nigeria. Similarly, the reps renewed their call for improved passenger service amid several delays and cancellations in June and July 2024 by asking the House Committee on Aviation to push for a policy that will introduce penalties for airlines that delay or cancel domestic flights without adequate consideration or support for passengers. However, efforts like these have yielded little or no results; as such, the fulfilment of this pledge will improve things and create a strong system that will strengthen passengers' rights.

promises.title: Expedite the passage of the Gas Flaring (Prohibition and Punishment) Bill to minimise the environmental and social impact of gas flaring in oil-producing areas.
promises.promise_blog:
Globally, Nigeria is ranked as one of the top ten countries that are endowed with natural gas with about 159 trillion cubic feet of natural gas reserve while about 2.5 billion cubic feet of gas in the country are reportedly flared by the numerous oil companies that are in the country.

 

In Nigeria, gas flaring has been a major concern for successive governments in the country due to the negative impact of the activities of oil companies flaring gas in the region on the environment and on the health of the people. There are about 2 million people living within 4km of gas flares, and a 2024 report by Humangle has revealed that the gas flares continue to kill crops, pollute water, and in many cases damage human health. Despite the existence of a regulatory framework to combat gas flaring in the country, there is little or no enforcement, and this has made the situation worse in recent years.

 

In May 2024, a resolution of the Nigerian Senate urged the Federal Government to ensure that the estimated $2million dollars per day being lost to gas flaring be converted and commercialized to fund the national budget conveniently without resorting to borrowing while also calling for an increase in the penalty of gas flares in the region.

 

Thus, in its legislative agenda, the 10th Assembly of the House of Representatives (HoR) pledged to expedite the passage of "the Gas Flaring (Prohibition and Punishment) Bill to minimise the environmental and social impact of gas flaring in oil-producing areas." To fulfil this promise, the HoR will have to ensure that such bill is passed within the timeframe it has set for it in its legislative agenda document. As we continue to witness adverse environmental issues in country, the passage of the bill will be a huge leap forward in address such problems.

promises.title: Collaborate with the Office of the National Security Adviser to Amend the Cybercrimes (Prohibition, Prevention, ets.) Act 2015
promises.promise_blog:
This pledge to work with the Office of the National Security Adviser (ONSA) to amend the Cybercrimes (Prohibition, Prevention, etc.) Act 2015 reflects the House of Representatives’ recognition that Nigeria’s cyber laws must keep pace with fast-evolving digital threats. While the 2015 Act was groundbreaking in tackling online fraud, cyberstalking, and identity theft, the digital landscape has since shifted dramatically.

 

Since 2015, new cyber threats—ransomware attacks, cryptocurrency-based scams, and AI-enabled fraud—have emerged, many of which are not fully addressed in the current Act. At the same time, parts of the law, such as certain provisions on cyberstalking, have drawn criticism for being used to target journalists and dissenting voices. Collaborating with ONSA allows lawmakers to combine legislative authority with national security expertise, ensuring that amendments close technical loopholes, improve investigative capacity, and provide safeguards against misuse.

 

For ordinary citizens, an updated Cybercrimes Act could mean stronger protection from online scams, more secure financial transactions, and clearer rules on data privacy in the digital space. If crafted with transparency and stakeholder input, it can also prevent overreach—ensuring that the fight against cybercrime doesn’t erode freedom of expression or privacy rights. This balance between security and civil liberties could make the reform one of the most practical, future-proof measures in the HoR’s agenda.

promises.title: Promise: Pass Legislation to Enforce Penalties and Sanctions for Breach of Legislative Summons
promises.promise_blog:
Legislative summons are an important part of ensuring effective lawmaking in the country, and they mostly require the representatives of the executives or that of ministries, departments and agencies (MDAs) to appear before the legislators for important meetings or questioning. The Nigeria constitution of 1999 gives power to the country's lawmakers to "expose corruption, inefficiency, or waste in the execution or administration of laws within its legislative competence and in the disbursement or administration of funds appropriated by it."

 

Furthermore, Section 89 (1c) of the constitution further empowers them to do it, however, summons have constantly disobeyed by the executive and even the MDA heads in recent year. This has prompt the 10th Assembly to prioritise the "passage of a legislation to enforce penalties and sanctions for breach of legislative summons" as on its medium-term promises. This means that the legislators aim to achieve this before October 2025.

 

Efforts to make this happen by previous assemblies have not achieved tangible results. According to the Coordinating Minister for Health, Prof. Muhammed Ali Pate, the BHCPF-funded primary health care facilities have been extended to over 10 million Nigerians who he said are receiving health care services through the fund.

promises.title: Amend the Constitution to Provide for Independent Local Government Election Commissions or Strengthen State Independent Electoral Commission (SIECs)
promises.promise_blog:
One of the most persistent weaknesses in Nigeria’s electoral system is the lack of credible, autonomous bodies to conduct local government elections. Currently, the 1999 Constitution mandates the existence of State Independent Electoral Commissions (SIECs) to run council elections, but in practice, it is widely perceived as an extension of state governments, often delivering one-party sweep results. This HoR’s proposal aims either to create constitutionally independent local government election commissions or to significantly strengthen SIECs’ independence, funding, and operational autonomy. 

 

Local government elections are the closest link between citizens and democratic governance, yet they are among the least trusted processes in Nigeria. Weak or compromised SIECs have contributed to voter apathy, opaque qualification processes, poor accountability at the grassroots, and the erosion of local government’s constitutional role. Amending the Constitution to insulate election commissions from state executive control, through secure tenure for commissioners, independent funding, and transparent appointment processes, could restore credibility to grassroots democracy. This rectification directly supports the legislative agenda’s broader goals of strengthening governance and enhancing citizen participation.

 

If implemented well, this change could produce more competitive, transparent, and credible local elections, giving citizens real choices and compelling elected councils to deliver on development mandates. However, the reform must be accompanied by clear criteria for appointments, robust oversight mechanisms, and enforceable penalties for political interference. Without these safeguards, new commissions could still face capture by political elites. Done right, this amendment could be one of the most transformative steps in the HoR’s agenda—revitalizing Nigeria’s third tier of government and making democracy more responsive where it matters most.

promises.title: Give Legal Backing to the National Renewable Energy and Energy Efficiency Policy (NREEEP).
promises.promise_blog:
Nigeria’s energy sector has for decades relied almost exclusively on fossil fuels, leaving households and industries vulnerable to erratic supply, high costs, and environmental harm. Recognising these challenges, the government introduced the National Renewable Energy and Energy Efficiency Policy (NREEEP) in 2015 as a framework to guide the transition toward cleaner, more sustainable energy. Yet, without the force of law, the policy has remained largely aspirational, with weak enforcement and inconsistent funding slowing its impact.  

 

If the 360-member Chamber gives NREEEP legal backing, it would transform it from a mere guideline into a binding national commitment. It would establish clear targets for renewable energy generation, enforce efficiency standards for appliances and buildings, and create incentives for private sector investment in solar, wind, biomass, and hydro power. More importantly, it would empower regulators to hold violators accountable, ensuring that energy projects align with Nigeria’s climate obligations under the Paris Agreement.  

 

The Nigerian legislature has both the constitutional authority and the responsibility to enact this reform. By embedding NREEEP into law, the National Assembly would provide a stable foundation for the reduced dependence on fossil fuels, and open new opportunities for green jobs and innovation.  

 

In doing so, it would demonstrate that the country is ready to match its aspirations with action, ensuring that sustainable development becomes more than rhetoric but a lived reality for its people.

The goal of the GGW was to restore about 100 million hectares of degraded land and to improve livelihoods across the Sahelian countries.

 

After the launch of GGW initiative, Nigeria retained a significant role as one of the pioneering countries. According to Humangle, Nigerian government began its Great Green Wall project in 2014, a project which stretched along 11 frontline states in Northwest and North-east of the country. in 2015, the National Great Green Wall Agency (NAGGW) was established by the federal government to "coordinate the tree planting process, management and installation of support services and provision of infrastructure such as solar systems and water for herders and farming communities."

 

Over the years, the NAGGW has received funding and support from national government and other transnational institutions like the Development of natural Resource Funds (DNRF), African Development Bank (AFDB), European Union and the World Bank. However, the enormity of the GGW and socio-economic impacts of the projects has necessitated calls for improved budgetary allocation and oversight from the lawmakers.

promises.title: Amend the Universal Basic Education Commission (UBEC) Act 2024 to Increase the Share of the Consolidated Revenue Fund Allocated to UBEC from 2% to 4%.
promises.promise_blog:
Education in Nigeria remains a top priority for any government. Thus, the country's education system is regularly guard-railed by legislation that focuses both on its qualitative and quantitative impact. The Universal Basic Education Commission (UBEC) Act is one of this legislations as it ensures that every children who are of primary and secondary school age in the country must be provided with free, compulsory and universal basic education.

 

Part 1 (sections 1-6) of the Act focuses on compulsory, free universal and basic education and the role of the government in ensuring its implementation by making education free, while Part III (section 11) of the Act explains the financing of the Universal Basic Education (UBE). According to the provisions of the Act, The implementation of the UBE shall be financed from "Federal Government block grant of not less than 2% of its Consolidated Revenue Fund." With the out-of-children number increasing yearly, one major consideration has been to increase funding for education in order to match current realities, hence, the promise by the Hon. Tajudeen Abbas-led 10th Assembly of the House of Representatives to "amend the Universal Basic Education Commission (UBEC) Act 2004 to increase the share of the Consolidated Revenue Fund allocated to UBEC from 2% to 4%."

 

Despite the provisions the UBE Act, primary and secondary education have faced significant setbacks in recent years as thousands of students continue to learn in dilapidated buildings, additional cost through levies have also prove to be a challenge for many parents in the country. In a November 2024 report, the Guardian Newspaper reported that figures from National Mass Education Programme Initiative (NMPI) and the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) showed no fewer than 18.3 million out-of-school are in the country.

 

The Executive Director of the Universal Basic Education Commission has also called for the amendment of the act as the commission continues to fight challenges that hinder the success of basic education in Nigeria.

 

“Having been enacted in 2004, that is 20 years ago, and given the developments and changes that have taken place in the society since then, it is our view that the Act is overdue for review. Our education should respond to the needs and aspirations of our country, and there is no better way to do this than being abreast of local and global developments," he said in an interview with journalists.

promises.title: Promise: Alter the Constitution to recognise Local Government as an independent tier with full Financial and Operational Autonomy.
promises.promise_blog:
The history of local governments (LG)in Nigeria and the quest to achieve full independence from the other tiers of government have been a long-standing issue in the Nigerian polity. Since the formal introduction of local government administration through the enactment of the Native Authority Ordinance of 1910, there have been countless number of reforms that have been pushed to ensure the smooth running of the closest tier of government to the grassroots. Hsitorically, it was the 1976 Guidelines for Local Government Reforms that birthed the current LG system in Nigeria, especially with the clear distinction of its basic structure and functions as the third tier of the government.

 

In 1999, after Nigeria's return to democratic rule, Section 7 (1) of the 1999 Constitution outline the current guidelines that the LG administration is based on. However, this has created so much debate with so many people calling for a review of the constitution. Amongst the issue being debated is the roles and responsibilities of the LGs in the country. Thus, the Tajudeen Abbas-led House of Representatives (HoR) through its Legislative Agenda document promised to embark on a political reform by reviewing the constitution to "alter the Constitution to recognise Local Government as an independent tier with full financial and operational autonomy. This will be done in consultation with States" within its first year.

 

To achieve this pledge, the HoR will have to present, consider and also pass a 1999 Constitution (Alteration) Bill specifically aimed at addressing this obvious lacuna which has stifle developments in the grassroots. In July 2024, the Spokesperson of the HoR, Hon. Akin Rotimi in an interview reiterated the house commitment to ensuring proper support is given to the LGs through the alteration of important parts of the constitution that limits it power.

 

"I must mention that the House of Representatives, the 10th Assembly, has a Legislative Agenda, and part of our objectives with the Constitution Review Committee is to ensure Local Government Autonomy," Rep. Rotimi explained. "Previous Assemblies have attempted this, but it didn't quite work. Now, with eight political parties represented in the 10th Assembly, we have a collective resolve to achieve this under the leadership of Rt. Hon. Abbas Tajudeen, "he said in an interview with Arise TV.

promises.title: Promise: Amend the National Security Agencies Act to expand membership of the two advisory councils (the National Defence Council and the National Secuirity Council) to include the Senate President and the Speaker in an observer capacity
promises.promise_blog:
The National Security Agencies Act (originally Decree No. 19 of 1986, later codified as Cap. N74, Laws of the Federation of Nigeria (2004) is the primary legislation that establishes and regulates Nigeria’s core intelligence and security agencies.  The act was promulgated in June 1986 as Decree No. 19 by the military administration of General Ibrahim Babangida. Its enactment was part of a wider security sector reorganisation, replacing the previous National Security Organisation (NSO) with three specialised agencies—the State Security Service (SSS), National Intelligence Agency (NIA), and Defence Intelligence Agency (DIA)—each with distinct mandates.

 

As it stands, the NSC and NDC are chaired by the President and include top executive and military leaders such as the Vice President, Minister of Defence, Chiefs of Defence and Army/Navy/Air Staff, and the National Security Adviser. This membership is strictly executive, with no formal role for legislative oversight. By introducing the Senate President and the House Speaker as observers, the reform would create a formal channel for legislative leaders to receive firsthand information on security assessments, defence policies, and intelligence priorities. While “observer” status does not grant voting rights, it allows Parliament’s top officers to better understand operational realities, which can improve budgetary appropriations, legal reforms, and oversight decisions. This change could also foster greater trust between the security establishment and elected representatives, reducing the current information gap.

 

This pledge could potentially improve accountability, but it must also give cognizance for the councils’ need for operational secrecy. Observer status should be clearly defined to prevent politicization or compromise of sensitive intelligence. With proper confidentiality safeguards, this change enhances legislative oversight without undermining the effectiveness of national security decision-making.
promises.description: Amend the National Security Agencies Act to expand membership of the two advisory councils (the National Defence Council and the National Secuirity Council) to include the Senate President and the Speaker in an observer capacity

promises.promise_blog:
Nigeria’s judicial system has long been plagued by delays, manual bottlenecks, and outdated infrastructure, leaving citizens frustrated and eroding confidence in the rule of law. Court records are often paper‑based, subjecting case files to loss or manipulation, and congested dockets mean litigants wait years for resolution. These inefficiencies undermine the constitutional guarantee of fair and timely justice.  

 

To address this, the government has pledged a budget for enhancing technology to expedite the digitisation of court processes and upgrade court infrastructure for swift and fair justice delivery. Digitisation and upgraded infrastructure will modernise courtrooms with ICT facilities and secure data systems, introduce electronic case tracking, digital archiving, and online access to judgments.   

 

The Nigerian legislature has already demonstrated its commitment to digital transformation. In November 2025, the National Assembly passed the National Digital Economy and E‑Governance Bill, jointly crafted by the Senate and House of Representatives, to revolutionise governance and embed ICT into public institutions. This landmark legislation shows that lawmakers recognise technology as a driver of efficiency and accountability. The National Assembly itself, comprising 109 Senators and 360 Members of the House of Representatives, has oversight powers to ensure that judicial reforms are properly funded and implemented.

promises.title: Promise: Pass an AI law to regulate artificial intelligence (AI) and ensure better conditions for the development and use of this innovative technology
promises.promise_blog:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) is regarded as the next frontier in technological evolution. According to Mckinsey and Company, artificial intelligence is a machine’s ability to perform some cognitive functions we usually associate with human minds. In Nigeria, the adoption and usage of AI has increased tremendously, with its usage ranging from personal usage, customer service, education, and manufacturing. Statista, the German market data and research company projected the AI market size in Nigeria to show an annual growth rate (CAGR 2024-2030) of 28.10%, resulting in a market volume of US$4.64bn by 2030.

 

Despite its potential and future prospects, especially for the country's emerging technological space, issues around data privacy, data vulnerabilities, and the potential biases in AI algorithms as well as ethical consideration are raising doubts among experts as the country is yet to pass any regulation around AI. According to AI Watch: AI Regulatory Tracker, there is currently no specific law or regulation that directly regulates AI in Nigeria, hence the importance of this pledge by the 10th Assembly of the House of Representatives.

 

While the development of AI in the continent is increasing, the adoption of AI policies and regulations by African countries is slow-paced. In terms of adoption, Mauritius is leading the pack, followed by Kenya and Egypt, while countries like South Africa and Nigeria have yet to adopt any AI regulation, making the fulfilment of this promise an important step towards aligning the country with the advancement of AI regulation in Africa. To keep this promise, the legislators are expected to expedite the passage of the current National AI Policy Draft.

Often times, it is the duty of the House of Representatives to uncover systemic weakness, policy gaps, or misconduct in public institutions. This responsibility is performed mainly using the facet of investigative hearings. For future reference by legislators,auditors, and the public, it is good practice to properly document these proceedings and track the implementation of recommendations. This ensures that findings are not lost after the media cycle fades and that identified reforms are followed through.

 

When investigative outcomes are preserved as part of the legislature’s historical record, they become a tool for institutional learning, and successive assemblies can consolidate on past knowledge and avoid repeating the same inquiries, measure progress on unresolved issues, and refine laws based on past findings.

 

In countries where legislative archives are well-maintained, these records have been instrumental in driving long-term reforms, especially in areas like procurement oversight, budget performance, and public sector ethics. For Nigeria, such documentation could bridge the gap between current governance challenges and sustainable policy solutions.

promises.title: Promise: Grant More Powers to State and Local Courts to Handle Issues Peculiar to their Regions, Reducing the Caseload of Federal Courts.
promises.promise_blog:
Justice in Nigeria is often stalled by a centralized judicial system. Ambiguities in the 1999 Constitution mean that cases that could be resolved at the state or local level such as small commercial disputes or local environmental issue are instead sent to federal courts. This jurisdictional confusion overburdens federal judges, resulting in a backlog of cases, lengthy trials, and significant delays that ultimately deprive citizens of timely justice.

 

By committing to a legislative review that expands the jurisdiction of State and Local Courts, the HoR aims to decongest the Federal High Court and other federal judicial bodies. It reflects the legislature’s intent to address delays in justice delivery—one of the most persistent criticisms of Nigeria’s legal system—and to make the courts more responsive to community-specific issues.  If upheld, it would allow State and Local Courts to resolve matters tied to regional realities—such as customary land disputes, local taxation, and environmental conflicts—without escalating to the federal level.

 

As the initiator of this reform, the HoR would need to lead constitutional amendments and statutory changes to clearly define jurisdictional boundaries, preventing overlap and forum shopping. It would also have to ensure that State and Local Courts receive adequate funding, judicial training, and infrastructure to handle their expanded roles effectively. If executed with these safeguards, the promise could strengthen public trust in local judicial systems, support regional autonomy in dispute resolution, and help build a more balanced national justice architecture.
promises.description: Grant more powers to state and local courts to handle issues peculiar to their regions, reducing the caseload of federal courts.

promises.title: Promise: Enact a law that promotes the education of children with special needs, ensuring they have access to quality education in inclusive settings
promises.promise_blog:
In its legislative agenda, the 10th Assembly of the House of Representatives (HoR) have promised to enact a law that will promote the education of children with special needs. This has become imperative in the wake of systematic deprivation they face.

 

If passed, this will put Nigeria among countries who are prioritising the education of those living with disabilities. For example, in the US, the US Department of Education described the country's "Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA) as a law that makes available a free appropriate public education to eligible children with disabilities throughout the nation and ensures special education and related services to those children, supports early intervention services for infants and toddlers and their families, and awards competitive discretionary grants. Similarly, Montenegro's 'law of Education of Children with Special Needs' described the education of children with special needs as an activity of the public interest.

 

In these laws that are obtained globally, children with special needs are described as "children with: physical, mental, and sensory disability; behavioural disorders; serious chronic diseases; emotional disorders; combined disorders; children ill for a long time, and other children who encounter difficulties in learning who need education by the educational programme with adjusted tuition and additional professional help, or by a special curriculum."

 

Currently, the country has several laws and policies that are related to the education of children with special needs, but stakeholders have continued to ask for intentional legislation that will propel inclusivity. For example, the Nigerian Child's Right Act, 2003, guarantees special protection measures for disabled children, but the provision of these measures is only subject to the availability of government resources. However, these existing laws have not effectively addressed the crucial problems that people living with special needs are subjected to daily as they also seek to get quality education.

 

By including this in its official agenda, the HoR is signalling that inclusive education for children with special needs is not just a social or moral cause, but a priority policy goal with legislative backing. Existing national laws, such as the Discrimination Against Persons with Disabilities (Prohibition) Act, 2018 and the Child Rights Act, 2003, contain provisions that touch on inclusive education, but they are fragmented, inconsistently implemented, and not tailored specifically to guarantee comprehensive access for children with disabilities. This pledge, therefore, positions the HoR to draft a dedicated education-focused law that would close gaps, consolidate protections, and set clear standards nationwide.

 

If enacted, such a law could create enforceable rights for special needs children to attend mainstream schools with appropriate support, thereby mandating teacher training, accessible infrastructure, learning aids, and individualized learning plans. It would also help dismantle systemic barriers, including exclusion from public schools and inadequate resourcing of special education units. Within the broader HoR legislative vision, this aligns with the goal of building an equitable education system that is regionally inclusive and reflective of Nigeria’s international commitments, such as the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDG 4 on quality education).

 

While this legislative promise is ambitious, its success will hinge on state-level buy-in and adequate budgetary provision. Many states of the federation have not yet domesticated even existing disability laws, and without clear compliance timelines, funding frameworks, and enforcement mechanisms, the initiative risks becoming another aspirational law with little ground impact. To maintain credibility, the HoR will need to embed accountability measures—such as annual progress reports to the National Assembly—and ensure that both the executive and state legislatures are engaged in its rollout. If these elements are built in, the promise could translate into a landmark reform for inclusive education in Nigeria.
promises.description: Enact a law that promotes the education of children with special needs, ensuring they have access to quality education in inclusive settings

promises.title: Mandate Representation of Young People in Decision-making Bodies, Such As Boards, Committees, And Councils, At All Levels Of Government
promises.promise_blog:
Nigeria today is one of the fastest-growing populations in the world. A vast majority of this population is under the age of 30. This demographic reality means that decisions made today will disproportionately affect young people for the longest time. Despite being the demographic majority, young people have historically been excluded from formal, high-level decision-making structures, often relegated to peripheral roles or youth wings of political parties. This exclusion contributes to widespread youth disillusionment and a feeling of being governed without sufficient input or understanding of the unique challenges that the youth face. 

While the Not Too Young To Run Act of 2018 lowered the age thresholds for elective offices, creating more opportunities for youth participation in elections, it does not extend to non-elective spaces such as boards, committees, and councils, where much of the policy shaping and institutional decision-making occurs. This underlines the importance of the legislative agenda's promise to mandate youth representation in such bodies across all tiers of government. 

This mandate would ensure that policies better reflect the realities of Nigeria’s youth, who face pressing challenges, including high unemployment, digital disruption, and climate vulnerability. Their perspectives are vital in shaping relevant policies and avoiding frameworks that are out of touch with the demographic that constitutes the backbone of the nation. Beyond inclusivity, youth representation enhances the democratic legitimacy of institutions; governance becomes more credible and participatory when it mirrors the age profile of society, rather than being dominated by a narrow elite.

Furthermore, ensuring that young people occupy meaningful seats in boards and committees would serve as a pipeline for grooming the next generation of leaders. Such participation provides valuable experience in policy development, oversight, and governance, creating a pool of well-prepared individuals who can take on larger responsibilities in the future. However, implementation must be designed to avoid tokenism, ensuring that youth representation is substantive rather than symbolic, and that appointees are selected on the basis of competence, merit, and inclusivity.

If properly enacted, this promise would not only expand inclusivity but also deepen democracy, build public trust, and unlock the innovative and energetic potential of Nigeria’s largest demographic group.

Open parliament is gradually becoming a standard practice across the world as more countries commit to open governance. 

 

According to the Open Government Partnership (OGP) ensuring "access to legislative information and creating mechanisms for public participation and accountability are critical to building an open, trusting relationship with citizens." It is against this backdrop that the Rt. This pledge aligns with the CSOs' and citizens' call for an open parliament which provides them the opportunity to monitor their elected representatives' activities. promises.promise_blog:
Shortly after the inauguration of the 10th Assembly of the Nigeria House of Representatives (HoR), the began a recommittal process for some bills that were passed in the previous assembly. Among the over 40 bills that were to be reconsidered was the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (Amendment) Bill 2023. In its Legislative Agenda, the HoR promised to ensure the passage of this within its first year.

 

The Economic Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) is the independent body that investigates and prosecutes financial and economic crimes in Nigeria and was established in 2004 to pursue this mission as the country intensified it fight against corruption. The EFCC Act requires the EFCC to enforce laws and regulations related to economic and financial crimes, including: the Money Laundering Act of 1995; the Money Laundering (Prohibition) Act of 2004; the Advance Fee Fraud and Other Fraud Related Offences Act of 1995; the Failed Banks (Recovery of Debts) and Financial Malpractices in Banks Act of 1994; the Banks and other Financial Institutions Act of 1991; the Miscellaneous Offences Act of 1985; the Criminal Code and the Penal Code and the Terrorism Act of 2011.

promises.title: Ensure the passage of National Electoral Offences Commission Bill to confer powers of the commission to prosecute electoral offences
promises.promise_blog:
Since Nigeria's return to democracy in 1999, successive elections have been marred with violence and other grievous electoral offences. With electoral infraction on the rise despite the recent electoral reforms and introduction of technology, there have been renewed calls for the creation of an independent Electoral Offences Commission that will be empowered to prosecute electoral offenders in the country.

 

To address this lingering problem, the 10th Assembly promised to "ensure the passage of the National Electoral Offences Commission Bill to confer powers of the commission to prosecute electoral offences" within its first year in office. Recalled that in 2007, an Electoral Reform Committee which was headed by Justice Mohammed Uwais (rtd), a former Chief Justice of Nigeria has recommended that an Electoral Offences Commission which is going to be a special prosecution body be established.

 

Also, there have been several attempts by previous assemblies to ensure the passage of the bill since 2019 but none has materialised. In July 2021, the Nigerian Senate passed a similar bill while in June 20, 2022, a similar bill passed second reading at the House of Representatives but failed to see the light of the day despite pressure from INEC and civil society agencies.

 

In January 2023, Mahmud Yakubu, the chairman of the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) raised concerns about the delay in the passage of the bill. He further stressed that the burden to arrest and prosecute is currently on his commission, which has a huge responsibility of organising elections. Although they have cooperated with security agencies, he said, the establishment of the commission would speed the effort to address the notorious sponsors of election malpractices in Nigeria.

promises.title: Consider and Pass Legislative Measures that will strengthen transparent and Competitive Processes for Public Procurement to Prevent Corrupt Update of Relevant legislation
promises.promise_blog:
When the House of Representatives says it will “consider and pass legislative measures that strengthen transparent and competitive processes for public procurement”, it’s tackling one of the most visible gateways to corruption in Nigeria—how the government spends public money. Procurement is where contracts are awarded, infrastructure projects are greenlit, and billions of naira change hands. Without clear, competitive, and transparent rules, this space can quickly become a breeding ground for embezzlement, inflated contracts, political patronage, and outright fraud. By putting this in its agenda, the HoR is signaling it wants to close those loopholes. 

Nigeria’s Public Procurement Act 2007 was a landmark law in its time, but 16 years on, the gaps are showing. Technology has evolved, but many procurement processes are still manual, opaque, and riddled with delays. Loopholes around “emergency procurement” and weak enforcement mechanisms allow questionable deals to slip through. Legislative updates could mandate digital procurement platforms, stricter competitive bidding rules, and stronger penalties for non-compliance—changes that not only save money but also build public trust.

 

For everyday Nigerians, stronger procurement laws translate directly into visible results—roads that last, hospitals stocked with the right equipment, and schools upgraded without budget padding. Transparent, competitive bidding cuts waste, reduces the chances of politically connected contractors walking away with inflated deals, and ensures public money works for the public. If the HoR backs this promise with real enforcement and open access to procurement records, it could turn one of the most corruption-prone areas of governance into a showcase for accountability and value for money.

promises.title: Promise: Enact comprehensive data protection legislation to ensure intelligence agencies handle personal data carefully and within legal boundaries.
promises.promise_blog:
In June 2023, the landmark Data Protection Act, 2023, was signed into law by Nigeria's president, Bola Ahmed Tinubu, after its consideration and passage by both the Senate and the Nigeria House of Representatives. One year after its passage, concerns around data protection still abound, especially with regards to the handling of personal data by the country's intelligence agencies. This prompt the Tajudeen Abbas-led House of Representatives to promise a comprehensive legislation that not only ensure the data protection but will also prioritise how personal data can be handled carefully and within legal boundaries by intelligence agencies.

 

Nigeria's attempt at comprehensive data legislation has been filled with gaps, which has continually left many with doubt. For instance, prior to the legislation of the Data Protection Act, 2023, the protection of personal data in Nigeria was regulated through a subsidiary regulation called the Nigeria Data Protection Regulation 2019. This legislation was issued by the country's national agency, National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA).

 

In a comprehensive review of the Data Protection Act, 2023 for Future of Privacy Forum, Mercy King'Or explained that the act contains unique provisions that should not be overlooked, including a new classification of data controllers and processors “of major importance” and specific obligations attached to them, as well as broader protections for exempt processing activities. Furthermore, it has been acknowledged that its full implementation would improve the business environment in the country, aligning it with global standards while also boosting the confidence of investors in the country. Yet, handling of citizens' data by intelligence agencies, which has raised eyebrows, is yet to be adequately addressed. Hence the importance of this legislation.

 

Including this reform in the House’s official agenda elevates it from a policy aspiration to a legislative priority. Intelligence agencies in Nigeria have broad investigative powers, but the absence of clear statutory boundaries creates risks of unlawful surveillance, data misuse, and breaches of privacy. By enacting a dedicated, comprehensive law, the HoR can guarantee that national security interests are balanced against constitutional rights, introduce judicial or parliamentary oversight for sensitive data handling, and establish penalties for unlawful breaches. This is especially critical in an era where digital communications, biometrics, and financial records are integral to everyday life, and where abuse of such data can have devastating personal and political consequences.

 

For the average Nigerian, this legislative promise offers a crucial safeguard against unchecked state surveillance and misuse of personal data. Intelligence agencies have, on multiple occasions, exceeded their legal limits—such as when the Defence Intelligence Agency acquired equipment capable of intercepting citizens’ calls and text messages without oversight and reports suggesting that state authorities monitored the communications of journalists, activists, and opposition figures under the guise of national security. A robust, comprehensive data protection law would establish clear legal boundaries, empower Nigerians with redress mechanisms, and introduce transparency and accountability in government data handling. Such a law would strengthen citizens' trust in public institutions and ensure that national security efforts don’t override individual rights—a landmark win for ordinary Nigerians in the digital age.
promises.description: Enact comprehensive data protection legislation to ensure intelligence agencies handle personal data carefully and within legal boundaries.

promises.title: Promise: Establish e-petition Systems to Allow Citizens to Submit Petitions Online
promises.promise_blog:
All over the world, parliaments are embracing e-petition as a means of enabling the public to express policy preference. This tool has gained wider significance as an effective tool for public participation. In a blog post for Digital Good Network, Lauren Martin, a PhD researcher, argued that parliamentary e-petitions enable the digital good because they provide an accessible platform for citizens to engage with and influence political processes at any time during the election cycle.

 

It is also worthy to note that e-petitions have been put forward as an important tool to facilitate good democratic governance. Hence, the importance of the pledge made by the Hon. Tajudeen Abbas-led 10th Assembly of the Nigeria House of Representatives (HoR) to "establish e-petition systems to allow citizens to submit petitions online." This particular system, according to the legislators, will be prioritise as one of its medium-term promises.

 

The importance of fulfilling promises like this holds high significance for many Nigerians who, on many occasions, do not have an appropriate channel to show their anger and dissatisfaction towards numerous policies that are believed to be anti-masses. Parliamentary e-petitions, on the other hand, are unique due to that 'institutional recognition' compare to social media channels. In many examples of the e-petitions found around the world, there are formal guarantees that deliberation and subsequent consideration of such petitions will follow once the petition has attained a threshold of signatures.

 

The House of Representatives is making a public commitment to strengthen democratic participation with this pledge. Unlike traditional paper petitions, which are limited by bureaucratic delays and restricted access, an online portal empowers Nigerians across regions to raise issues, propose reforms, and seek redress directly from their parliament. Embedding e‑petitions into the legislative process could transform reactive oversight into genuine two‑way interaction between the electorate and its representatives. Within the broader agenda, it aligns with other transparency and accountability promises, positioning the HoR as a more accessible, responsive body that values direct input from Nigerians.

 

In today's increasingly digital world, tools like this have proven potent to address the deep gap in democratic engagement and will be useful in shaping policymaking in Africa's most populous nation, should it be achieved.

 

For ordinary Nigerians, this could mean greater access to lawmakers, a transparent process for tracking petitions, and a legitimate channel for influencing legislative priorities. The key will be ensuring the platform has follow-through—meaning that petitions meeting set thresholds trigger parliamentary responses. If executed well, this agenda item could be one of the most visible, citizen-focused successes of the current House.

This promise signals that the HoR intends not only to legislate but also to back its priorities with funding for research institutions, universities, and innovators working on health breakthroughs.

 

Investment in tropical disease research can lead to better diagnostics and treatments for illnesses that are often neglected by global pharmaceutical companies. Supporting traditional medicine research can help validate and standardize indigenous remedies, integrating them safely into mainstream healthcare. Funding vaccine development and innovative treatments builds national capacity to respond to outbreaks—reducing reliance on costly imports and slow international supply chains, as witnessed during COVID-19. This multi-pronged focus aligns with both public health needs and Nigeria’s aspiration to become a regional leader in medical innovation.

 

If fully implemented, this agenda item could lead to tangible improvements in everyday healthcare—more accessible treatments, quicker responses to disease outbreaks, and recognition of local medical knowledge. It could potentially also open opportunities for Nigerian scientists to drive global research in health fields traditionally dominated by other regions. The key will be ensuring transparency in fund allocation, measurable research outcomes, and collaboration between government, academia, and the private sector. If done right, this promise could shift Nigeria from being a consumer of medical solutions to a creator of them, transforming both national health security and the economy.

promises.title: Legislative Measures to Require the FJSC to Conduct Written Tests and Interviews Rather than NJC
promises.promise_blog:
The Federal Judicial Service Commission (FJSC) is primarily tasked with advising the National Judicial Council (NJC) on judicial appointments and recommending the discipline or removal of judicial officers. It holds the authority to manage personnel in specific courts and is empowered to perform various functions conferred by law.

 

The NJC on the other hand has power to appoint and exercise disciplinary control over Judicial Officers, power to collect, control and disburse all monies, capital and recurrent, for the Judiciary and to deal with all matters relating to Policy and Administration.

 

Section 153 (I) of the 1999 Constitution establishes the FJSC. Furthermore, FJSC is empowered to advise the NJC but FJSC does not conduct written tests and interviews. In a 2023 report by UNODC, vast majority of respondents that were engaged in the research criticized the lack of transparency in the method of evaluation of candidates, with many raising specific concerns about the lack of clarity about why some applicants were invited for interviews while others were not.

 

Furthermore, the UNODC interview with vast majority of respondents who are lawyers and judicial officials also criticized the lack of mandatory written and oral examinations of candidates. As this issue lingers, the Legislative Agenda of the tenth assembly, the Tajudeen Abbas-led  House of Representatives pledge to propose legislative measures to require the FJSC to conduct written tests and interviews rather than the NJC to address the lack of transparency and removal of the non-merit based system that is currently used to select justice in the country.

promises.title: Strengthen the Electoral Act to ensure that all cases are resolved and judgments made before the date of swearing-in
promises.promise_blog:
Strengthening the Electoral Act so all election cases are resolved before swearing-in would close one of Nigeria’s biggest democratic loopholes: today, presidential (and many gubernatorial) petitions often conclude months after inauguration, when incumbency advantages are already entrenched. In 2023, the Presidential Election Petition Court delivered judgment on September 6, 2023, and the Supreme Court affirmed the result on October 26, 2023, well after the May 29 swearing-in. This is a recurring issue; the 2007 presidential dispute similarly concluded long after the winner had assumed power.

Why is this a problem? Once sworn in, a president controls appointments, the machinery of state, security and information flows, and benefits from the symbolic power of office. Scholars and observers have long warned that post-inauguration litigation can skew incentives and tilt outcomes toward incumbents, thereby eroding public confidence in judicial independence. 

Nigeria’s current timelines (Electoral Act 2022) set filing/hearing windows, but do not guarantee completion before inauguration, which is why cases routinely outlast swearing-in. 

There are workable African models. Kenya’s Constitution (Art. 140) requires the Supreme Court to hear and determine a presidential petition within 14 days, and swearing-in waits for that decision.  Zambia gives its Constitutional Court 14 days to conclude a presidential petition, a strict deadline intended to resolve disputes before the inauguration. Zimbabwe likewise requires the Constitutional Court to resolve any presidential challenge under Section 93, with the inauguration following the court outcome. 

Adopting a Nigerian variant of these “pre-inauguration closure” rules would reduce uncertainty, curb incumbency distortions, and bolster the legitimacy of winners.
promises.description: Strengthen the Electoral Act to ensure that all cases are resolved and judgments made before the date of swearing-in

promises.promise_blog:
The issue of gender (in)equality is a reoccurring one within Nigeria's evolving political landscape. Political office holders, civil society organizations, as well as organised women groups have all recently joined the call for gender equal opportunities, especially the inclusion of women in political and decision-making processes. In the Legislative Agenda document released by the 10th Assembly of the Nigeria House of Representatives, the lawmakers also pledged to 'Pass a Gender Equal Opportunities Bill (GEOB)' as part of its commitment to gender equality.

 

Over the years, the complexities and dynamics of Nigerian politics have made it hard for women to actively participate or get elected for political positions both at the national and sub-national levels. Several political analysts and commentators have also pinpointed the significant role gender-based societal and political bias plays as a roadblock to women's participation in politics across different levels in Nigeria. About half of the country's population is female, with about 110 million female population, yet, the participation among this group has been terribly low since the country's return to democracy in 1999.

 

In the run off to the 2023 general election in Nigeria, only a meagre 8.9% of the total candidates were women. After the election, only 48 women out of the 1,019 females that contested in the country's state houses of assembly elections won, representing a 4.7 percent success rate for women. Previous elections in 1999, 2003, 2007, 2009, 2011, 2015, and also 2019 also witnessed the ostracization of women in politics. The last presidential election had only one female presidential candidate out of the 18 political parties that fielded candidates.

promises.title: Pass the Electoronic Surveillance & Communications Privacy Bill to Restrict Wire Taps from Telephone Calls and Transmissions of Electronic Data by Computer
promises.promise_blog:
Electronic surveillance and communications privacy issues are quite complex, and in recent years, they have become a top issue in national discourse in the wake of technological sophistication and increasing usage of digital innovations in governance and other sectors of the country. In one breath, mass digital or electronic surveillance by the government has been pinpointed as a tool to target activists, journalists, and political opponents in the country, while on the other hand, unlawful violations of privacy and social media monitoring of citizens have led to renewed conversation around breach of citizens communication privacy.

 

Nigeria's weak legal framework - despite the existence of laws such as The Cybercrimes (Prohibition, Prevention, etc.) Act, 2015; The Nigerian Communications Act, 2003 and The Data Protection Regulation (NDPR), 2019 - around these two important issues has led to the call for an improved legislation that will ensure strict oversight. Hence, the importance of the pledge made by the 10th Assembly of the House of Representatives (HoR). In its legislative agenda document, one of the medium-term pledges of the Rt. Hon. Tajudeen Abbas-led HoR is to "pass the Electronic Surveillance & Communications Privacy Bill to restrict wire taps from telephone calls and transmissions of electronic data by computer."

 

A report published by HumAngle in February 2023 detailed how domestic surveillance agencies in Nigeria have continued to violate citizens' privacy through electronic surveillance and wiretapping of calls. The report detailed how the Nigeria Police Force arrested two journalists in 2019 over what is believed to be a report published on a local new platform, News Digest. According to the report, the two journalists; Gidado Shuiab and Alfred Olufemi, after the phone of a former News Digest employee was bugged.

 

In 2020, Al-Jazeera reported that Nigerian intelligence bought a tool to spy on citizens, raising deeper concerns around privacy. In recent times, citizens and journalists who participated in protests have been tracked down and arrested after their mobiles were hacked. According to Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR, systematic surveillance of people in the public space online and offline (...) constitutes an interference with the right to privacy and can have highly detrimental effects on the enjoyment of other human rights. In June 2024, Paradigm Initiative, a leading organisation fighting for digital rights, uncovered the sale of citizens' data online for as little as N100, raising concerns around a serious breach of privacy and data protection in Nigeria.

 

The fulfilment of this pledge will be very pivotal and will eventually set the country on the right direction in its digital privacy aspiration.

promises.title: Establish Legislative Liason Desks/Information Centres in SHAs to give Citizens Access to Legislative Resources Information and Assistance.
promises.promise_blog:
By including this in its agenda, the House of Representatives is signaling an intent to bridge the gap between citizens and their legislature in a practical, on-the-ground way. State Houses of Assembly (SHAs) are often the first port of call for constituents with concerns, yet access to legislative information and services remains fragmented. Dedicated liaison desks or information centres would serve as formal hubs where citizens can obtain legislative documents, track bills, submit petitions, and get guidance on how to engage with lawmakers.

 

These centres could demystify the legislative process and make it more accessible. A farmer in a rural area could learn how to contribute to a bill affecting agriculture; a small business owner could access procurement guidelines; a civil society group could track committee activities relevant to their advocacy. By decentralizing access to legislative resources, the HoR would not only promote transparency but also foster a culture of active citizenship where people see themselves as stakeholders in lawmaking.

 

If implemented seriously, these centres could become one of the most visible and citizen-friendly reforms in the HoR’s agenda—turning legislative access from a privilege for the few into a right for all. Furthermore, it can improve the quality of legislation itself, as lawmakers will receive more direct and localized feedback from their constituents. Ultimately, this move helps to ensure that the House of Representatives' legislative agenda is truly people-centered and reflective of the diverse needs and concerns of Nigerians across the country.
promises.description: Establish legislative liason desks/information centres in SHAs to give citizens access to legislative resources information and assistance.
