promises.title: Work with the Executive to Amend the Student Loan (Access to Higher Education) Act, 2023, to Include the Provision of Scholarships and Financial Aid for Students pursuing Technical Education.
promises.promise_blog:
The House of Representatives’ plan to work with the Executive to amend the Student Loan (Access to Higher Education) Act, 2023 is more than a minor policy adjustment—it is an expansion of opportunity. As it stands, the Act largely benefits university students, leaving aspiring technicians, artisans, and vocational specialists without comparable support. By prioritizing this amendment in its legislative agenda, the HoR is making a clear statement that technical and vocational pathways are equally critical to national development and merit the same level of financial assistance as traditional academic degrees.

 

Technical and vocational education is a cornerstone of industrial growth, job creation, and innovation. Extending scholarships and targeted financial aid to students in these fields would enable young Nigerian, regardless of background, to acquire in-demand skills in areas such as renewable energy, ICT, advanced manufacturing, and infrastructure development. This approach not only reduces unemployment and the national skills gap but also strengthens Nigeria’s position in an increasingly competitive global economy.

 

If implemented effectively, this amendment could transform access to technical education by ensuring that financial constraints do not block talented individuals from pursuing their chosen careers. For communities, it would mean a stronger pool of trained professionals; for the economy, a more agile and self-reliant workforce. Success will depend on transparent administration, merit-based allocation, and alignment with labour market demands.  

 

If the HoR delivers on this promise, it could help redefine Nigeria’s education-to-employment pipeline and create long-term benefits for both individuals and the nation.
promises.description: Work with the Executive to amend the Student Loan (Access to Higher Education) Act, 2023, to include the provision of scholarships and financial aid for students pursuing technical education.

promises.title: Promise: Revisit the Labour Act to Ensure Increased Opportunities for Women and Delete Sections that Empower a Minister of Labour to make Regulations Prohibiting or Restricting Women's Employment
promises.promise_blog:
With the advancement in modern workforce, there has been a call from several stakeholders for the legislators to review the outdated Labour in Nigeria. Aside from from being an impediment in the fight against casualisation of workers, the law also limit equality especially with the section that empower a minister of Labout to make regulations prohibiting or restricting women's employment in certain industry.

 

This is why the 10th Assembly of the Nigerian House of Representatives have pledged to delete that particular section (Sections 55, 56 and 57 of the Nigeria Labour Act of 2004) and also increase opportunities for women. For example, Section 56 empowers the Minister of Labour to make regulations that may prohibit or restrict the employment of women in certain types of work or under certain conditions. 

 

Earlier this year, the Director-General of the NIgeria Employer's Consultative Association (NECA), Adewale Smatt Oyerinde call on the legislators to swiftly pass a new labour law. “Stabilising a robust labour framework is paramount. It will not only regulate activities within the labour sector but also set the tone for fairness and justice in all employment relationships," he said during an interview with Punch NG.

 

In another opinion editorial by Samuel Jekeli of Centre for Social Justice on Cable Newspaper, he also called on the national assembly to amend the outdated labour laws in order to address the endemic issues of labour rights violations and injustice in the country. Therefore, amending this outdated law is an important pledge of this 10th Assembly.
promises.description: Revisit the Labour Act to ensure increased opportunities for women and delete sections that empower a minister of Labout to make regulations prohibiting or restricting women's employment

promises.title: Promise: Amendment of the Constitution to Enable President to Reject Recommendations where Objective Public Complaints and Objections are Raised Against the Recommended Candidates and Request for Another Recommendation
promises.promise_blog:
Currently, the President is constitutionally required to nominate candidates—such as Ministers, judicial officers, and heads of federal commissions—for Senate confirmation, with limited formal means to reject a nominee based solely on public outcry or credible objections. This proposed constitutional amendment would institutionalise the President's ability to act on objective public concerns, transforming a historically opaque process into one that respects both democratic checks and the voice of citizens.

 

This amendment elevates transparency and legitimacy in appointment processes as it ensures that valid, well-documented public objections—such as allegations of corruption, ethical violations, or serious conflicts of interest—cannot be dismissed or ignored. Instead, the President could formally request an alternate nominee, signalling responsiveness to public sentiment. This check could deter the presentation of unsuitable candidates in the first instance and strengthen public confidence in the integrity of our institutions. The formal inclusion of this power would help Nigeria approach an ideal where appointments are not just constitutional formalities but reflect merit and earned public trust.

 

While enhancing accountability, it’s vital to avoid politicising or paralysing appointment mechanisms. The amendment must clearly define what qualifies as an “objective public complaint,” establish procedures for validating such objections, and set reasonable timelines to prevent perpetual delays in filling key positions. Without these safeguards—such as a designated oversight committee or independent review mechanism—there’s a risk this provision could be misused to block legitimate nominees or become a tool for political gamesmanship. Implemented judiciously, however, it offers a meaningful step toward inclusive and accountable governance.
